lead: Sinusoidal PWM compares a low-frequency sine reference with a high-frequency triangular carrier. The comparator output drives the bridge, so the switch duty ratio changes sinusoidally across the output cycle. The fundamental then follows the reference, while the unwanted harmonics move up to the carrier frequency and its sidebands. This is the standard way to make a fixed DC bus behave like a variable-voltage, variable-frequency AC source. It is used in motor drives, UPS units, solar inverters and small domestic inverters.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 and Chapter 4.3 for H-bridge operation and notch-based voltage control; Unit 1 for switching loss that sets the carrier frequency.

blocks.text: An inverter bridge can apply only fixed DC rails or zero. To make a sine wave, the switches are turned on and off many times in every output cycle. Let v<sub>ref</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin(2π f<sub>m</sub> t) be the sine reference. V<sub>m</sub> is its peak in V and f<sub>m</sub> is its frequency in Hz. A triangular carrier of peak V<sub>c</sub> and frequency f<sub>c</sub> is compared with this reference. When v<sub>ref</sub> is greater than the carrier, the comparator output is high. The duty ratio d therefore changes across the f<sub>m</sub> cycle, and the average bridge voltage follows a sine.
m<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> / V<sub>c</sub>,  m<sub>f</sub> = f<sub>c</sub> / f<sub>m</sub>
blocks.where: m<sub>a</sub> is the modulation index; V<sub>m</sub> is the sine reference peak in V; V<sub>c</sub> is the triangular carrier peak in V; m<sub>f</sub> is the frequency ratio; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in Hz; f<sub>m</sub> is the reference frequency in Hz.

blocks.text: For a full bridge, the average output over one carrier period is V<sub>dc</sub>(2d − 1). With d = 0.5 + 0.5 m<sub>a</sub> sin θ, this average equals m<sub>a</sub>V<sub>dc</sub> sin θ. The fundamental peak is m<sub>a</sub>V<sub>dc</sub> and the fundamental rms is m<sub>a</sub>V<sub>dc</sub>/√2. The linear range is m<sub>a</sub> ≤ 1. Above 1 the reference cuts the carrier peak, so the comparator saturates and low-order harmonics appear.

items: Choose f<sub>m</sub> from the load, for example 50 Hz for a motor.
Choose f<sub>c</sub> from switching loss and filter size; a higher f<sub>c</sub> gives smaller filters but more loss.
Set m<sub>a</sub> for the required fundamental voltage.
Compare the sine and triangle and send the pulses to the gate drive.

blocks.text: Bipolar PWM uses one sine reference and one triangular carrier. The two legs of the full bridge switch as diagonal pairs. When the comparator is high, the output is +V<sub>dc</sub>; when it is low, the output is −V<sub>dc</sub>. There is no zero state. The output is a two-level PWM wave whose average follows the sine reference. The fundamental peak is m<sub>a</sub>V<sub>dc</sub> in the linear range.

The unwanted harmonics are grouped around the carrier frequency and its sidebands. The first cluster is near m<sub>f</sub>f<sub>m</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>, with sidebands at f<sub>c</sub> ± 2f<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>c</sub> ± 4f<sub>m</sub> and so on. A low-pass filter after the bridge removes this cluster. If m<sub>a</sub> is pushed above 1, the output becomes overmodulated. The fundamental then rises slowly towards the square-wave value 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π, but low-order harmonics grow quickly. Most designs stay at or below m<sub>a</sub> = 1 unless extra voltage is essential.

Unipolar PWM uses two sine references 180° apart, or one reference compared with two carriers. Each leg is switched independently. The bridge output can then be +V<sub>dc</sub>, 0 or −V<sub>dc</sub>. When both upper switches are on, the load sees 0 V; when both lower switches are on, it also sees 0 V. The differential output still has the wanted sine fundamental, but the ripple pulses come twice per carrier period. The first harmonic cluster moves from near f<sub>c</sub> to near 2f<sub>c</sub>. At the same carrier frequency, the output filter can be smaller because the ripple is at a higher frequency.

Third-harmonic injection adds a common third-harmonic component to the three-phase references. A common choice is one-sixth of the fundamental amplitude. The phase reference peak falls, so the sine reference can be made larger before it hits the carrier. In a three-phase inverter this allows m<sub>a</sub> up to 2/√3 ≈ 1.15 before clipping. The line-to-line fundamental rises by about 15%, while the third harmonic cancels in the line-to-line voltage. Beyond 1.15, overmodulation begins and low-order harmonics return.

figure.caption: The comparator turns the sine and triangle into gate pulses; the bridge then applies the DC bus. The example values are m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8, f<sub>m</sub> = 50 Hz, m<sub>f</sub> = 21, so f<sub>c</sub> = 1.05 kHz.

spec.title: Sine-triangle PWM
spec.aria: A sine reference with ma 0.8 and fm 50 Hz and a triangular carrier with mf 21 enter a comparator, whose output drives the gate drive and full bridge to make the PWM output.

examples.question: A single-phase full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V. It uses sinusoidal PWM with f<sub>m</sub> = 50 Hz, m<sub>a</sub> = 0.8 and m<sub>f</sub> = 21. (a) Find the fundamental peak and rms output voltage. (b) Find the carrier frequency and the first harmonic cluster for bipolar PWM. (c) State where the first cluster moves with unipolar PWM.
steps: Carrier frequency f<sub>c</sub> = m<sub>f</sub>f<sub>m</sub> = 21 × 50 = 1050 Hz = 1.05 kHz.
Bipolar PWM puts the first cluster near f<sub>c</sub> = 1.05 kHz.
Unipolar PWM cancels the odd carrier ripple, so the first cluster moves near 2f<sub>c</sub> = 2.10 kHz.
examples.answer: The fundamental is 320 V peak, 226.3 V rms; f<sub>c</sub> is 1050 Hz; unipolar PWM moves the first cluster near 2100 Hz.
examples.check:
import math
Vdc = 400.0
ma = 0.8
fm = 50.0
mf = 21.0
V1p = ma * Vdc
V1rms = V1p / math.sqrt(2)
fc = mf * fm
fc_unipolar = 2 * fc
print(V1p)
print(round(V1rms, 1))
print(fc)
print(fc_unipolar)

traps: Swapping m<sub>a</sub> and m<sub>f</sub>. m<sub>a</sub> sets voltage; m<sub>f</sub> sets the harmonic position.
Using the peak fundamental m<sub>a</sub>V<sub>dc</sub> as an rms value. Divide by √2 for a sine rms.
Assuming unipolar and bipolar PWM have the same spectrum. Unipolar pushes the first cluster to about 2f<sub>c</sub>.
Believing m<sub>a</sub> can rise far above 1 without distortion. Above 1 the comparator saturates and low-order harmonics appear.
Forgetting that third-harmonic injection is a three-phase common-mode trick. It helps line-to-line voltage, not every single-phase load.

quiz.q: Define the modulation index m<sub>a</sub> and the frequency ratio m<sub>f</sub> for sine-triangle PWM.
quiz.a: m<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/V<sub>c</sub>, the sine peak divided by the carrier peak. m<sub>f</sub> = f<sub>c</sub>/f<sub>m</sub>, the carrier frequency divided by the reference frequency.

quiz.q: Why does sinusoidal PWM move the unwanted harmonics to a high frequency?
quiz.a: The bridge switches many times per reference cycle. The low-frequency sine is made by the average duty, while the fast switching creates the ripple. That ripple sits near the carrier frequency and its sidebands, not near the 50 Hz fundamental.

quiz.q: A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V, m<sub>a</sub> = 0.6, f<sub>m</sub> = 50 Hz and m<sub>f</sub> = 15. Find the fundamental peak and the carrier frequency.
quiz.a: V<sub>1p</sub> = m<sub>a</sub>V<sub>dc</sub> = 0.6 × 600 = 360 V. f<sub>c</sub> = m<sub>f</sub>f<sub>m</sub> = 15 × 50 = 750 Hz.

quiz.q: Compare the output spectrum of bipolar and unipolar PWM at the same carrier frequency.
quiz.a: Bipolar PWM has its first harmonic cluster near f<sub>c</sub>. Unipolar PWM has zero states and its differential ripple appears near 2f<sub>c</sub>. The unipolar filter can therefore be smaller, but more gate signals and dead time are needed.

quiz.q: What happens to the output when m<sub>a</sub> exceeds 1?
quiz.a: The sine reference cuts the carrier peak for part of the cycle. The comparator saturates and the output becomes overmodulated. The fundamental rises towards 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π, but low-order harmonics grow. The linear relation m<sub>a</sub>V<sub>dc</sub> no longer holds.

quiz.q: State the linear modulation limit for sine-triangle PWM.
quiz.a: m<sub>a</sub> ≤ 1. Above 1 the modulator is overmodulated.

quiz.q: What does third-harmonic injection achieve in a three-phase inverter?
quiz.a: It adds a common third harmonic to the phase references. The phase peak falls, so m<sub>a</sub> can reach about 1.15 before clipping. The line-to-line fundamental rises by about 15%, and the third harmonic cancels in line-to-line voltage.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real drives add dead time to prevent shoot-through, and that dead time distorts the low-order voltage at light load. Digital PWM uses timers and shadow registers so the duty update happens once per carrier period. Random PWM and discontinuous PWM are used to spread acoustic noise or cut switching loss. Search for dead-time compensation, discontinuous PWM, and SiC inverter PWM if you meet a practical design problem.
